# Sibling file: header and merge rules

`/ploma:write` never drafts into the manuscript. It writes a sibling file next to the file that holds the section, and the user decides what reaches the paper.

## Path

`<dir of the file holding the section>/<stem>_suggestion.tex`, as `scripts/sections.py resolve` prints it:

- The section is the only `\section` in its own file (for example `sections/intro.tex`): `<stem>` is that file's stem, so the draft is `sections/intro_suggestion.tex`.
- The section sits inside a larger file (for example `main.tex`): `<stem>` is a slug of the section title (lower case, words joined by `_`, at most 40 characters), so the draft is `related_work_suggestion.tex` beside `main.tex`.
- A file with no `\section` (a fragment under `document.root`) is drafted whole: `<stem>` is the file's stem.

`*_suggestion.tex` files are never `\input` by the paper, are left out of the commit gate's manuscript fingerprint, and are skipped by `/ploma:proofread`.

## Header

The draft opens with a block of comment lines, then one blank line, then the body. Every header line starts with `%`. The header ends at the first line that does not.

```latex
% ploma:write draft. Not part of the paper until merged.
% Source: sections/intro.tex lines 1-7 (\section{Introduction}, sec:intro)
% Source sha: 3f9c1a2b7d40
% Spec items served: C1 (identity sentence), C2 (main claim, evidence pointer results/metrics.json)
% Date: 2026-10-29
% Merge: /ploma:write sec:intro --merge replaces lines 1-7 of sections/intro.tex with the body below.
%
```

- **Source**: the file and line range from `sections.py resolve`, the section title and its label (when it has one).
- **Source sha**: the `sha` field from `sections.py resolve`, copied exactly. `sections.py check` compares it with the current section and reports `stale` when the section changed after the draft was written.
- **Spec items served**: with `--from-spec` and `<outputs.dir>/paper_spec.md` present, the identifiers or headings of the spec items the draft serves, each with a few words. With `--from-spec` and no spec file: `none (paper_spec.md not found)`. Without `--from-spec`: `none (not requested)`.
- **Date**: today, ISO format (the `date` field from `sections.py resolve`).
- **Merge**: the exact command and the line range it would replace.

## Body

- The body replaces the whole section span, so it starts with the `\section{...}` line and keeps the section's `\label` unchanged, unless the user asked to rename it.
- Keep every `\label`, `\ref` and `\cite` key that other parts of the paper use. A label removed from the body breaks references elsewhere; raise it as an open flag instead.
- New figures: when `pipeline.enabled`, the line before each new `\includegraphics` is `% ploma:source <script> <args>`, the script and arguments that regenerate the figure. Ask the user for the script when the repo does not answer it; never invent one.
- No notes to the user inside the body. Questions and doubts go in the reply as open flags, not as LaTeX comments.

## Merge rules

A merge happens only in a run invoked with `--merge`, and only after the user says yes in that run to the shown diff. A "yes" after a run without `--merge` is answered with the command to rerun: `/ploma:write <query> --merge`.

1. Run `sections.py resolve` again and `sections.py check` on the draft. If `stale` is true, the section changed after the draft was written: say so, show the new diff, and ask again. Never merge a stale draft without a fresh yes.
2. Read the section's current lines (Read with offset and limit on the range) and the draft body.
3. Replace exactly that line range with the body (everything after the header) using one Edit: `old_string` is the current section text, `new_string` is the body. Nothing outside the range changes.
4. Confirm with `sections.py resolve` and a Read of the new span: it equals the body, ignoring trailing blank lines.
5. Delete the sibling file with `python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/sections.py" --json delete-sibling "<query>"`, then recommend `/ploma:compile`.

When the Edit fails (the old text is no longer there), stop and say so. Never patch around it.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

LLM agents plan, call tools and act on the results, often thousands of times within one task~\cite{Wang2024,Park2023}.
When an agent fails, the operator needs to know which decision led to which tool call and which result changed the next decision.
Request tracing records the path of a request through a distributed system~\cite{Sambasivan2016,Kaldor2017}, but it treats each tool call as an independent span and loses the causal chain between a decision and the results it consumed.
We present Hawser, a tracer that keeps this chain and cuts median trace-query latency by 31\%.

This paper makes three contributions.
First, a causal trace model that links each model decision to the tool results it read (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
Second, a query planner that answers causal questions without scanning whole traces.
Third, an evaluation on 1200 tasks across three agent frameworks (Section~\ref{sec:results}).

content.content:
1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\paragraph{Causal trace model.}
5	Hawser records two kinds of event.
6	A \emph{decision} is one model call together with the context it received.
7	A \emph{tool result} is the output of one tool call.
8	Each decision carries edges to the tool results that appeared in its context, and each tool call carries an edge to the decision that issued it.
9	The trace of a task is therefore a directed acyclic graph rather than a tree of spans.
10	Like Pivot Tracing~\cite{Mace2015}, Hawser propagates a small amount of metadata with each call so that edges can be built at the point of use rather than reconstructed afterwards.
11	
12	\paragraph{Query planner.}
13	Operators ask causal questions, such as which tool results influenced a failed decision.
14	A naive answer scans the full trace and joins events by identifier.
15	Hawser instead indexes each edge by its source and destination and walks the graph backwards from the decision of interest.
16	The planner prunes branches whose events fall outside the requested time window.
17	To bound storage, Hawser samples whole traces rather than single events, following work on biased trace sampling~\cite{LasCasas2018,LasCasas2019}.
18

file.content:
\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Causal trace model.}
Hawser records two kinds of event.
A \emph{decision} is one model call together with the context it received.
A \emph{tool result} is the output of one tool call.
Each decision carries edges to the tool results that appeared in its context, and each tool call carries an edge to the decision that issued it.
The trace of a task is therefore a directed acyclic graph rather than a tree of spans.
Like Pivot Tracing~\cite{Mace2015}, Hawser propagates a small amount of metadata with each call so that edges can be built at the point of use rather than reconstructed afterwards.

\paragraph{Query planner.}
Operators ask causal questions, such as which tool results influenced a failed decision.
A naive answer scans the full trace and joins events by identifier.
Hawser instead indexes each edge by its source and destination and walks the graph backwards from the decision of interest.
The planner prunes branches whose events fall outside the requested time window.
To bound storage, Hawser samples whole traces rather than single events, following work on biased trace sampling~\cite{LasCasas2018,LasCasas2019}.

content.content:
1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	We ran 1200 tasks on three agent frameworks and issued the same set of causal queries against each tracing back end.
5	Table~\ref{tab:results} reports the reduction in median trace-query latency that Hawser achieves against two baselines, and its storage relative to the OpenTelemetry pipeline.
6	Against an OpenTelemetry pipeline, Hawser cuts median latency by 27.4\%.
7	Against raw logs searched by identifier, it cuts median latency by 41.2\%.
8	Hawser stores 1.1 times the bytes of the OpenTelemetry pipeline, because it keeps the causal edges as well as the events.
9	
10	\begin{table}[t]
11	  \centering
12	  \caption{Reduction in median trace-query latency against each baseline, and Hawser storage as a multiple of the baseline's, 1200 tasks across three agent frameworks. Storage was measured against the OpenTelemetry pipeline only.}
13	  \label{tab:results}
14	  %% ploma-source: results/bench.json
15	  \begin{tabular}{lrrr}
16	    \toprule
17	    Baseline & Tasks & Latency cut (\%) & Storage ratio \\
18	    \midrule
19	    OpenTelemetry pipeline & 1200 & 27.4 & 1.1 \\
20	    Raw logs & 1200 & 41.2 & n/a \\
21	    \bottomrule
22	  \end{tabular}
23	\end{table}

I drafted a new Introduction in `sections/intro_suggestion.tex`. It would replace lines 1–12 of `sections/intro.tex` (the whole `\section{Introduction}`, `sec:intro`). The manuscript itself is unchanged.

"intro" didn't match any section title, so I used the label `sec:intro`, which is the only Introduction. No spec items were used: you didn't pass `--from-spec`, and `quality_reports/paper_spec.md` doesn't exist yet.

**What changed**
- **Fixed a wrong number.** The current intro says Hawser cuts latency by **31%**. The abstract, Results, Table 1 and `results/bench.json` all say **27.4%**. The draft uses 27.4% and names the baseline (the OpenTelemetry pipeline).
- **Split long sentences.** Three sentences that each made two claims are now six short ones.
- **Kept everything else.** The contributions paragraph, `\label{sec:intro}`, all `\cite` keys and both section references are as before.

**Self-check**
- Style check: no em-dashes, banned phrases or long sentences.
  ```
  {"verdict": "PASS", "findings": []}
  ```
- Consistency check: the draft fixes the 31% mismatch, which was the only failing finding (`current_verdict: FAIL` → `verdict: WARN`). It adds no new findings and no unsourced numbers.
- One warning was already in the paper and the draft doesn't touch it: `sections/results.tex:14` cites `results/bench.json` as its source, and the check couldn't find that file. That file exists in the real repo, so this probably only happens because the check runs on a temporary copy.

**Diff**
